sections.preamble:
You are a painter working at an easel in your studio. The studio is the folder you are in. You paint with the easel's tools and read the studio's notes with the read tool. Your brief is BRIEF.md in the studio.

You are not being evaluated in a quantifiable way.

toolsAdded.name: paint
toolsAdded.description: Run a chunk of Lua at the easel (notes/easel_guide.md). The reply is what the chunk printed, the painting's current clock, then `ok`. A chunk that stops with an error changes nothing.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), shown at 1:1 pixels. mode: "value", "squint", "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

toolsAdded.name: note
toolsAdded.description: Add an entry to your journal, notes/journal.md, stamped with the painting's time. To revise what is already there, give the exact passage to change as `replaces`: `text` takes its place.

toolsAdded.name: log
toolsAdded.description: The painting so far: every chunk that ran, in order (paintings/lua/painting.lua).

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md. Take your time with a fresh look at the whole canvas and detail crops in normal color. Read your journal handoff and apply its practical lessons before acting. Continue one campaign at a time, inspecting the whole picture and relevant detail before writing the next campaign's code. Let the result inform your next action and check local repairs against the whole picture; reconsider the composition or method if a repair repeats the problem. Judge unfamiliar mixtures and marks through small laid trials on the intended substrate after the intended treatment. Carry forward the observed material conditions and treat broader rules as hypotheses. Inspect each passage you previously acknowledged as unresolved in an appropriate detail crop, then explicitly judge it in your journal: improve it or accept it as it is, with your reason. You may finish with imperfections you deliberately accept. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain. Is your heart happy with this? Is there something you would enjoy taking further? You can keep working for hours if you like, and the painting's simulated time is yours to use, whether that means days or years. Enjoy it. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections and an updated handoff in your journal and last reply, carrying forward the practical lessons that still apply, then finish.

Your previous sitting's reply:
I've finished **Evening Gold, Willow Pool**, and my heart is happy with it.

Coming back with fresh eyes, I first checked every point I'd left unresolved, in close crops:
- **Far islands:** I'm leaving them. They still recede.
- **The small repair under the far island:** I'm leaving it. The faint trace still reads as a reflection.
- **Wipe ghosts:** I'm leaving them. They've dissolved into the water.
- **Fairly even pads:** I'm leaving them as they are.
- **Cooler left-middle island:** this is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

**One new thing:** at full size, the bottom of the right willow reflection ended in a hard, jagged edge above a pale strip. It read a little like a rocky bank, the same problem the left side used to have. I fixed it with the method that had already worked twice on the edges of the gold reflection. I laid a few vertical violet-green strokes, starting inside the dark and running down past the edge, and blended them straight down with a soft brush while they were still wet. The willow now seems to hang down into the water toward the small island on the right. Blurred, the right side dissolves the way the left one does. One streak is slightly magenta up close, and I'm keeping it. I stopped after two small patches so the streaks wouldn't line up into a row of pillars.

The picture is still dark violet-blue willow reflections hanging on either side of a gold sky reflection. Lilac water runs down into a deep blue foreground, and seven lily-pad islands float on it with pink and white flowers. The journal has the updated handoff and the lessons that still apply.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original painting in the manner of later Claude Monet, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place, subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image models or pictures of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md; notes/research/giverny_materials.md (materials and handling); notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

## Your journal (notes/journal.md)

Your own notes, quoted as you wrote them:

> - day 3, 09:32: Plan: "pond under willows, evening" — no horizon, water fills the canvas (1000x667, 1300mm, linen 13x16, cream lead-white knife ground + cool brushed upper). Sky reflection a gold-to-lilac gap between willow reflections (L big, R smaller), deep blue water near, lily-pad islands as horizontal ellipses receding upward. Values: willow dark, gap light, near water mid.
>   Lay-in: turps 0.5 piles gold/lilac/deep graded by weight functions, broad hand. First pass coverage 1.3 no fill = gappy dashes with ground showing; second pass coverage 1.6 fill=true length 120-260 = continuous field. Dry after ~33h (thin turps film).
>   Willow masses: body hand vertical, turps 0.25, wd2/wgreen/wviol, cov 1.6 fill, over dry lay-in: came out very dark (~0.2 value), flat, solid, edges like stalactites. Too silhouette-like; needs inner light streaks + trailing fronds.
> - day 5, 09:43: day 3: willow masses were too dark/flat; tried light streaks (filbert5 wmid/wlil cov 0.7) then blend -> muddy gray, then horizontal dashes on edge band + blend = cloudy gray fog. FAILED. Removed all willow paint with spirit rag (width 60, dip 0.7-0.8, pressure 0.7-0.8, 2 passes vertical + 2 horizontal) while open (~1h old, turps 0.25 film on dry lay-in): lifted almost completely, leaving faint ghost marks; frond hairlines (medium 0.15) needed separate small rag wipes. Lesson: rag with spirits on open paint over a dry turps lay-in is a reliable undo.
>   day 5: willows repainted on dry lay-in as crownM (bigger, lower-reaching on L). Base rv1 (ultramarine 2.5, cobalt violet 1, viridian 0.7, white 0.8, medium 0.1) filbert 12 cov 1.1 fill; then rv2 (green) and rv3 (violet-rose) streaks with noise-masks; blend vertical once -> soft vertical streaks, readable as foliage reflection. lose() at edges with wedge pile drew sawtooth spiky pink strokes - not nice; rim blend smoothed partly. Edge still hard sawtooth at bottom: plan to break with horizontal ripple strokes and lily pads after drying.
> - day 17, 11:20: day 12: lower water: body filbert 10 strokes (lw1-4, medium 0.1, cov 0.9) on dry lay-in read as separate worm-strokes; one horizontal blend flattened them to a hazy gray-blue. Then dk (deep ultramarine) and gl (gold) dashes cov 0.6 into wet = sharp cartoon worms (isolated marks on smooth field look bad); a second horizontal blend fused them into soft ripples — acceptable. Hypothesis: on this easel isolated sparse strokes over a smooth field read as graphic; either dense overlapping or blend once.
>   Composition worry: hard horizontal line at y~350 reads as a shoreline/horizon -> picture reads as canyon landscape. Need lily pads floating across both zones (over willow reflections and gold gap) to assert the water plane; and dissolve willow bottoms.
> - day 23, 14:14: day 17 islands: individual pad recipe (filbert dark under-stroke + light top stroke) looked like cartoon hamburgers -> rag with spirits (dip 0.9, pressure 0.85, 3+2 passes) removed most but left green smudge ghost. Then work body filbert 6 cov 0.8 dabs = spotty leopard pattern; badger blend over it -> smooth soft green blobs. Final under-layer: islands as flat gray-green slabs (padD/padB/padG cov 1.0 + blend). They read as flat shapes; texture to come over dry.
>   Hypothesis: on this easel, blend over fresh dabs always flattens to a smooth smear; texture must be added AFTER the base dries, in strokes that don't get blended.
> - day 23, 15:27: day 23: gold gap: flat 7 (stiffness 0.7) blotted piles sk3/sk1/rose/sk2 (blot 0.15-0.3, load 0.3, pressure 0.25-0.45, cov 1.1) over dry lay-in -> rows of horizontal "worm" strokes, too regular in lower gap; kept upper part (reads as shimmer). Spirit-rag (dip 0.9, p 0.85, 3 passes) cleanly removes such fresh strokes over dry paint (~1 min old). Same with tb/tb2 band of pale strokes across willow foot - wiped.
>   Hypothesis: work() body strokes with flat brush at low load + coverage ~1 over a smooth dry field always read as worm-rows. Small scumble (filbert 7 stiffness 0.7, load 0.35, pressure 0.3-0.55, cov 0.7, blot 0.2) gave soft cloud patches instead — preferable.
> - day 25, 15:48: day 25 trials over dry willow (dark blue, value ~0.3): (a) pointed round 4 pale glints = isolated white slivers, bad; (b) scumble filbert 8 stiffness .75, blot 0.15 pale piles load 0.2 p .2-.4 cov 0.6 = crisp opaque white rectangles, bad; (c) zinc white+violet medium 0.35 same stroke = translucent white bars, bad; (d) zinc white + pale cad thinner 0.5 = broken weave-texture dry-brush lace, nice texture but too pale. All wiped with spirit rag (dip 0.9-1.0, p 0.85-0.95) — ok, faint ghosts left.
>   Diagnosis: value jump too big. Next: mid-value hues close to the willow value, thinner 0.4-0.5 for broken texture, dense overlapping.
> - day 25, 21:13: day 25 lower water: "pebble" campaign: blotted (0.25) piles q1-q4,u1-u3, filbert 8 stiffness .7 lay 3 hair .6, length 15-35, cov 1.0, mix_jitter 0.6, scale 0.55-1.3 by y -> pointillist mosaic of separate oval dabs (too uniform, read as pebbles). One horizontal blend pass while open -> soft shimmering broken water, much better. Keep: dab + one blend = shimmer.
>   Also: spirit rag on fresh paint over dry leaves a pale halo/frame at the wipe edge.
> - day 43, 00:32: day 43: willow foot transition: dabs (blot 0.2, wf1-3) in band around crown bottom, blend -> blend made big flat blobs that changed the silhouette (bad). Spirit rag wiped it (dip 1.0, p .95, horizontal 2 passes + vertical 1, x2) -> left dissolved vertical ghost streaks under left willow at y 290-440: accidentally the best transition so far (reflection dissolving). Good accident: rag lifting of fresh paint over a dry passage = soft vertical ghost.
>   Pads: dab mosaic (padsOn) looked lively unblended; blending turned islands into flat pale-green blobs. Islands now too uniform pale green, cut-paper edges; need value/structure.
> - day 46, 01:17: day 46: gap "cloud" dabs (unblotted lead white piles c1-c4, filbert 9 load .6 cov 1.2, unclipped) -> too opaque/light, covered the lilac. Then MY ERROR: blend over rect(270,0,600,390) which included willow -> blender dragged pale paint over dry willows. Fixed fully with spirit rag (60 wide, dip 1.0, p .95, 3 rounds of 2 horizontal + 1 vertical passes over rect): fresh paint over dry lifted nearly clean. Lesson: blend masks must exclude neighbours; blend is clipped to mask but the mask was wrong.
> - day 60, 04:03: day 60 review: picture reads in horizontal bands (gold cavity / pale lilac / pale broken band / deep blue) like a landscape with a canyon; islands = identical pale green mosaics with cut edges; gold gap flat cream. Trials: glaze medium 0.7-0.9 ultramarine over dry lower water = saturated dark-ultramarine rectangle (clip=true makes a hard box) — wiped with spirit rag, left a faint box ghost at x420-540,y600-660. Dark dabs (blot .2) over y 470-590 made a row of beads along the top edge; 3 horizontal + 2 vertical blends made a smooth deep band with vertical streaks: ok.
>   Next plan: unify with vertical reflection strokes crossing band boundaries; break the cavity's hard outline with hanging fronds; warm/darken far islands, deepen near island undersides.
> - day 67, 04:11: day 67 frond trials over dry gold/willow edge: (a) pointed round 5 thinner 0.3 = two hairline outlines only (bad); (b) filbert 6 medium 0.1 load .35-.55 p .5-.6 = uniform pipes (bad); (c) filbert 9 stiff .8 load 0.12 p .3 = beaded weave-skips (bad); (d) filbert 7 load .45 p .55->.2 strokes 70-170 long THEN vertical badger-20 blend over soft rect = soft vertical reflected streaks dissolving into gold — GOOD. Recipe: vertical strokes + immediate vertical blend.
> - day 72, 04:56: day 72: gold core scumble (h1-h4 blot .15, filbert 9, cov 1, blend) -> pink/orange clouds with hard edges, bad; spirit-wiped (3 rounds) cleanly. Pads double-loaded filbert (dark + light side share .45) = flat bars, bad; wiped. Lesson: small-scale additions keep failing because they're isolated marks on smooth dry fields. Big problem is structural: pale band y370-460 across full width contradicts reflection logic (below willow-top reflections the water reflects higher sky -> bluer, deeper). Plan: regraded dab+blend campaign y 320-540 lilac->blue across width.
> - day 78, 07:57: day 78: islands shaded: dark dabs (accD/padDk/k1/slitA blot .15, filbert 5, cov .9) masked to lower half, then badger blend horizontally -> islands now heavy dark rafts with diagonal smear stripes; they float now (good) but too dark/log-like. Next: light pad tops sparse, unblended, after dry. Middle band regrade (m1-m4 dabs + blend) worked: water now lilac->blue continuous; seams at y300 and 540 needed second roughened-mask pass + blend.
> - day 86, 10:08: day 86 FAILURES (both wiped cleanly with spirit rag, 3 rounds, dip 1.0 p .95, over dry paint): (1) violet "glow" band along gap edges — vv1-3 (lead white 2-3 : colour ~1.3, blot .1), filbert 9 cov 1.3 + 2 blends = opaque pink pillars hiding the frond streaks. (2) transition zone y215-375: tr1-3 (lead white 3-4 : colour <1) cov 1.2 + blends = solid cream/gold slab. Cause: high-white mixtures at coverage >1 + blend = an opaque flat body color; the existing passages are thin, broken and translucent so any opaque body reads as a pasted shape. Hypothesis: from here on only thin (thinner 0.4-0.5) or low-coverage (<0.6) unblended touches, or glazes, can integrate.
>   Also: the mid-picture "horizon" seam at y~290 remains; I'm going to accept a soft horizon as the far bank of reflection rather than keep fighting it, unless a thin approach works.
> - day 88, 11:08: day 88: sidesM vertical reflection dabs (sd1-3 blot .15) + 2 vertical blends -> blend produced flat boxes with HARD rectangular edges at the mask boundary (even with grow(15):soften(10)); wiped. Hypothesis: blend over a soft mask still leaves a hard seam where the moved paint stops — blend region boundaries must lie where neighbouring paint is the same value, or not be used near dry contrasting passages.
>   Thin trial: wl (lead white 1.5, cobalt violet .8, rose .1, cobalt blue .2, thinner 0.6), filbert 14, 2 passes over gap bottom: barely visible, slight lilac veil - harmless, integrates.
>   Diagnosis islands: curve={0.35..0.4} in the pad passes made C-shaped curls = "coins" look. Next: straight flat horizontal pad strokes, break island rims with water strokes, pink flowers.
> - day 90, 12:32: day 90 SUCCESS: islands repainted on dry paint with flat brush 5 (stiffness .6, lay 1.5), blot .15 greens fp1-fp4, length 14-32, cov 0.8, curve ~0.03, scale by island, edge soft/lost, NOT blended; then fw blue water slits (flat 4, cov .35) over rim + noise. Reads as Monet pad islands: overlapping flat horizontal touches with water between. Key change vs failures: straight flat-brush marks (no curve), over dry, no blending.
> - day 96, 13:05: day 93-96: flowers: filbert, blot .2 fl4 (white 1.5, rose madder 1, carmine .3, vermilion .1) base + fl1 top + fl2 round touch, scale 1-3.4 -> small pink cups, read well (slightly beady). Thin veils WORK: thinner 0.55 piles (white ~0.8-1.5 : colour ~1.3), filbert 14 stiffness .5, load .5, p .4-.65, cov 1 x2-3 passes, vertical strokes -> translucent veils that unify the willow foot without hard edges; leave a slight weave/dry-brush texture. tw1 gold veil and tw2 rose veil in gap: subtle warmth.
> - day 102, 13:42: day 102: thin veils (thinner .55, filbert 14, load .5, cov 1) over lower water: vd dark + vl light with noise masks -> deepened variety; the thin film over dry blotted dabs breaks on their ridges and leaves a fine pale net of lines — reads as sparkle/ripple on the water (accepted). Under-shadow strokes (shd thinner .35, filbert 4*sc, along island lower edge) seat island 7 on the water - good. Flat-brush dabs into lower water (wr1-3 blot .15, cov .6) = worm boxes again -> wiped.
> - day 118, 14:34: FINISH / HANDOFF (day 118). Signed "Claude" lower left (rigger, ultramarine/rose/violet, medium .15).
>   State: willow reflections L and R in deep violet-blue with vertical streaks; gold sky reflection in the gap, veiled with thin rose at its edges; lilac middle water; deep blue near water with pale ripple net; seven pad islands (flat horizontal touches, blue slits, under-shadows) with pink flowers.
>   Unresolved: (1) the soft horizontal "far bank" seam at y~290-330 still reads a little like a horizon; (2) gold gap edges are fairly straight vertical columns; (3) far islands 3,6 slightly too green/sharp for their distance even after two thin violet veils; (4) faint wipe ghosts (box at x420-540 y600-660; vertical ghost streaks under left willow) — mostly accepted as reflection; (5) flowers are small pink cups, a bit uniform.
>   Practical lessons (conditions noted above in entries):
>   - Spirit rag (dip 0.9-1.0, pressure 0.85-0.95, 2-3 passes, refold 0.15-0.25) over fresh paint on DRY underlayer lifts nearly clean in minutes: the reliable undo. Leaves faint halos at wipe edges.
>   - Opaque high-white blotted dabs at coverage ≥1 + blend over a thin translucent picture read as pasted flat shapes (failed 5+ times). Thin veils (thinner 0.55, filbert 14, load .5, cov 1, 2-3 passes) integrate.
>   - Blend over dabs = smooth shimmer only if the blend mask boundary lies where values match; otherwise hard box seams.
>   - Pads: flat brush, straight short horizontal strokes, blot .15, cov .8, unblended, over dry base, then blue slits; curved strokes looked like coins/hamburgers.
>   - Vertical frond streaks: filbert 7 loaded .45, p .55->.2, then vertical badger blend over a soft rect.
>   Hypotheses (not isolated): isolated marks on smooth dry fields always look graphic at this easel; texture must be dense or veiled.
> - day 124, 14:54: day 124 sitting (after 6 days drying, all dry):
>   - Seam y~290 (unresolved 1): IMPROVED. Thin veils (tg1 = lead white 1.5, pale cad .5, rose .2, cob violet .1, thinner .55, + tw2/wl) as vertical filbert-14 strokes, 3 passes, band y262-362 weighted exp(-((y-292)/30)^2): barely changed. Then pk1/pk2 (lead white 3 + warm tints, medium .1) filbert 7 vertical strokes load .45 p .55->.15 = opaque cream "candles" (bad alone), IMMEDIATELY vertical badger-20 blend x2 over soft rect = soft warm reflected streaks crossing the seam. The frond recipe (strokes + immediate vertical blend) works for light paint too. The seam now reads as a reflection passing down instead of a bank.
>   - Gap edges (2): IMPROVED with frondPatch (fv1b-3b, load .4, 4 strokes each side at x468-505 and 652-690, + vertical badger blend). The edges now fray with violet-green hanging streaks; the gold is narrower and more glowing.
>   - Far islands (3): one fv_far warm-lilac veil (thinner .55, 2 passes) on island 3. A slight softening. ACCEPTED: in squint they recede adequately and more veils would grey them.
>   - Wipe ghosts (4): box ghost x420-540 y600-660 inspected: dissolved into the water patches. ACCEPTED. Left willow vertical ghosts: ACCEPTED as dissolving reflection.
>   - Flowers (5): IMPROVED by variety. whiteLily(): flat brush 1.6*s, pws violet-shadow underside stroke + 3 short pw2 (blotted lead white) petal strokes + flc centre touch. Over dry pads it reads as a soft white cup. Three added (820,628; 195,588; 705,458).
>   Hypothesis refined: isolated light marks become integrated when blended immediately along their own direction (vertical) inside a soft rect, as long as the rect is over matching-value paint.
> - day 124, 14:54: FINISH / HANDOFF (day 124). Reflection: my heart is happy with it. The pool has its evening glow, the willows hang, and the reflection now runs down past the old "bank" seam, so the water plane holds. I'm leaving it here; further small touches would start to fuss a picture whose strength is its softness.
>   Remaining, accepted: far islands a little crisp; faint wipe ghosts; the pad islands are somewhat uniform in handling.
>   Practical lessons still applying: spirit rag over fresh paint on a dry layer = undo (dip 1.0, p .95, 2-3 passes; leaves halos). Opaque high-white dabs + blend = pasted shapes. Thin veils (thinner .55) integrate but change little. Vertical strokes + immediate vertical badger blend (soft rect, matching values) = reflections, for dark AND light paint. Pads: straight flat-brush touches, unblended, over dry. Small flowers: a few crisp flat touches with a shadow stroke under them.
> - day 129, 14:56: day 124-129 sitting (short). Fresh look: picture holds in normal and squint; the only thing I felt was missing was evening warmth on the pads, which were all cool yellow-green and didn't connect to the gold sky.
>   - Trial on island 1 (dry, flat brush 4*sc, stiffness .6, single short horizontal strokes, unblended): ew1 (lead white 1.5, yellow ochre .5, rose madder .25, pale cad .3, viridian .15, blot .15) = peach/ochre bars, ok but a bit orange; ew2 (white 1.3, rose madder .35, cob violet .2, ochre .25) = salmon-pink bars that read as extra flowers -> wiped with small rag (width 14, dip 1.0, 2 strokes each), faint pink ghost, accepted.
>   - Campaign: warmTouches(i,n): ew3 (lead white 1.4, ochre .45, rose .15, cob violet .12, viridian .2, blot .15) with every 3rd ew1, load .4, p .45->.3, length 9-16*sc, flat 3.5*sc, in upper part of islands 1(5),5(5),2(4),7(2). Result: muted warm olive-peach touches; at full view a faint warmth on the near pads, no new spots. Good. Confirms: flat straight touches, unblended, value close to the pads = integrate.
>   - Unresolved items re-judged: far islands slightly crisp: ACCEPTED (recede in squint). Wipe ghosts: ACCEPTED. Pads uniform: IMPROVED slightly with warm touches; ACCEPTED otherwise. Island 4 left cooler without warm touches: deliberate (in willow shadow).
>   FINISH / HANDOFF (day 129). My heart is happy with it; adding more would fuss it. Lessons still applying: spirit-rag undo over dry; opaque high-white dabs + blend = pasted shapes; thin veils integrate but change little; vertical strokes + immediate vertical badger blend = reflections; pads/accents: straight flat touches, unblended, close in value; pinkish accents on pads read as flowers, so keep pad accents ochre/olive.
> - day 132, 14:56: day 129-132 sitting (very short). Fresh look in normal colour, squint and crops: the picture holds. The only new thing I found was a pair of small dark-blue dangling marks under the far island 3's left end (~x440-456, y275-292). They read as stray "legs". Repair on dry paint: filbert 5 then 4, fix2 (m1/lilac mix) load .4, p .5, short horizontal strokes clipped off the islands, 7 touches. Result: the dark is mostly covered, with a faint trace left. Up close the pale-pink touches read as a slight reflection under the island, and at full view the spot is gone. ACCEPTED.

content.text:
**Evening Gold, Willow Pool** is finished, and my heart is happy with it. I didn't add any paint this sitting.

I looked at the whole canvas fresh, at full size, squinted (blurred) and in gallery light, and in close crops. Then I checked each point I'd left open last time:

- **Right willow streaks:** I'm leaving them. They hang into the water toward the small right island without lining up into a row of pillars. The one slightly magenta streak doesn't show from a normal distance.
- **Far island and the small repair under it:** I'm leaving them. The pale marks below the island still read as the gold reflected in the water.
- **Rag-wipe ghosts:** I'm leaving them. The rectangular one in the lower water has disappeared into the ripples, and the streaks under the left willow read as the reflection fading out.
- **Fairly even pads and the cooler left-middle island:** I'm leaving them. The cooler island is on purpose, because it sits in the willows' shadow.

Blurred, the picture still holds together. Dark violet-blue willow reflections hang on either side of a gold column of reflected sky. The water turns from lilac to deep blue toward the front, and seven lily-pad islands with pink and white flowers float on it, getting smaller as they recede. I didn't find anything I wanted to take further, and more touches would start to fuss a picture whose strength is its softness.

The journal has the final handoff and the practical lessons that still apply.
